intro.source: 10 questions about Lessons 11–15. Take your time. You can look back at the lessons and try again as often as you like.
intro.back: 10 questions about Lessons 11–15. There is no need to rush. You can look at the lessons again and try again as often as you want.

questions.0.question.source: Each Vessantara panel shows a different episode. What is an episode?
questions.0.question.back: Each Vessantara panel shows a different episode. What is an episode?

questions.0.options.0.text.back: The writing that is on a panel

questions.0.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. Writing on an object is an inscription. An episode is one part of a story. Look back at Lesson 11.
questions.0.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite. Writing on an object is an inscription. An episode is one part of a story. Look at Lesson 11 again.

questions.0.options.1.text.source: One part of a longer story
questions.0.options.1.text.back: One part of a longer story

questions.0.options.1.feedback.source: Yes. Chapter 2 and Chapter 3 show two episodes from the same story.
questions.0.options.1.feedback.back: Yes. Chapter 2 and Chapter 3 show two episodes from the same story.

questions.0.options.2.text.source: The wood the paint is on
questions.0.options.2.text.back: The wood that the paint is spread on

questions.0.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. The panels are painted on teak wood. An episode is one part of a story. Look back at Lesson 11.
questions.0.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite. The panels are painted on teak wood. An episode is one part of a story. Look at Lesson 11 again.

questions.1.question.source: The Thai panels have inscriptions that name donors. What do the inscriptions tell us?
questions.1.question.back: The Thai panels have inscriptions that name donors. What do the inscriptions tell us?

questions.1.options.0.text.source: Who asked for the panels to be made
questions.1.options.0.text.back: Who asked for the panels to be made

questions.1.options.0.feedback.source: Yes. Named donors asked for them, for religious reasons. We know this, even with no names for the painters.
questions.1.options.0.feedback.back: Yes. Named donors asked for the panels to be made, for religious purposes. We know this, even though the painters' names are not known.

questions.1.options.1.text.source: The names of the painters who made them
questions.1.options.1.text.back: The names of the painters who made them

questions.1.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. The museum has no names for the painters. The inscriptions name the donors. Look back at Lesson 11.
questions.1.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite. The museum does not know the painters' names. The inscriptions name the donors. Look at Lesson 11 again.

questions.1.options.2.text.source: The year when the story first began
questions.1.options.2.text.back: The year the story first came into being

questions.1.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. The story is much older than the panels. The inscriptions name the donors. Look back at Lesson 11.
questions.1.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite. The story is much older than the panels. The inscriptions name the donors. Look at Lesson 11 again.

questions.2.question.source: The workers in The Harvesters are idealised. What does idealised mean?
questions.2.question.back: The workers in The Harvesters are idealised. What does idealised mean?
questions.2.question.note: "Idealised" is "diidealkan", the form Lesson 12 and this course's TERMS.md use (flagged there).

questions.2.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. Bruegel painted it for a rich trader. Idealised means shown as better than real life. Look back at Lesson 12.
questions.2.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite. Bruegel painted it for a rich trader. Idealised means shown as better than real life. Look at Lesson 12 again.

questions.2.options.1.text.source: Shown just as they really lived
questions.2.options.1.text.back: Shown exactly as their lives were

questions.2.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. That is the opposite. Idealised means neater and more perfect than real life. Look back at Lesson 12.
questions.2.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite. That is the opposite. Idealised means neater and more perfect than real life. Look at Lesson 12 again.

questions.2.options.2.text.source: Shown neater than in real life
questions.2.options.2.text.back: Shown neater than they really were

questions.2.options.2.feedback.source: Yes. The workers look neater and better than they did in real life. It is one view of farm life.
questions.2.options.2.feedback.back: Yes. The workers look neater and better than their real lives. It is one view of life on a farm.

questions.3.question.source: Why did Millet begin to make prints like The Gleaners?
questions.3.question.back: Why did Millet begin to make prints like The Gleaners?

questions.3.options.0.text.source: Partly to earn money and find buyers
questions.3.options.0.text.back: Partly to get money and buyers

questions.3.options.0.feedback.source: Yes. Prints helped Millet reach buyers. Many of them were middle class.
questions.3.options.0.feedback.back: Yes. Prints helped Millet reach buyers. Many of them were middle class.

questions.3.options.1.text.source: To copy a painting by Bruegel
questions.3.options.1.text.back: To copy a painting by Bruegel

questions.3.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. Millet's print is his own work, made almost 300 years after Bruegel. Look back at Lesson 12.
questions.3.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite. Millet's print is his own work, made almost 300 years after Bruegel. Look at Lesson 12 again.

questions.3.options.2.text.source: Because a rich patron ordered just one
questions.3.options.2.text.back: Because a rich patron commissioned just one

questions.3.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. A print is made in many copies for many buyers. Millet made prints partly to earn money. Look back at Lesson 12.
questions.3.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite. A print is made in many copies for many buyers. Millet made prints partly to get money. Look at Lesson 12 again.

questions.4.question.source: What does Monet's painting of Argenteuil show in one picture?
questions.4.question.back: What does Monet's painting Argenteuil show in one picture?

questions.4.options.0.text.source: A busy city street with no trees
questions.4.options.0.text.back: A busy city street without trees

questions.4.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. The painting shows a river path with trees and boats. Look back at Lesson 13.
questions.4.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite. The painting shows a riverside path with trees and boats. Look at Lesson 13 again.

questions.4.options.1.text.source: Boats and trees, and factories far off
questions.4.options.1.text.back: Boats and trees, and factories in the distance

questions.4.options.1.feedback.source: Yes. Fun on the river and factory chimneys share one scene. Nature and people's work are not split apart.
questions.4.options.1.feedback.back: Yes. Fun on the river and factory chimneys share one scene. Nature and people's work are not separated.

questions.4.options.2.text.source: Farm workers cutting grain in a field
questions.4.options.2.text.back: Farm workers harvesting grain in a field

questions.4.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. That is The Harvesters. Argenteuil shows a river town near Paris. Look back at Lesson 13.
questions.4.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite. That is The Harvesters. Argenteuil shows a riverside town near Paris. Look at Lesson 13 again.

questions.5.question.source: In The Railway, a woman faces us and a girl looks through a fence. What can a careful viewer say?
questions.5.question.back: In The Railway, a woman faces us and a girl looks through a fence. What can a careful viewer say?

questions.5.options.0.text.source: What the two people are thinking
questions.5.options.0.text.back: What the two people are thinking

questions.5.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. The painting cannot show their thoughts. We can only guess. Look back at Lesson 13.
questions.5.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite. The painting cannot show their thoughts. We can only guess. Look at Lesson 13 again.

questions.5.options.1.text.source: What they said to each other
questions.5.options.1.text.back: What they said to each other

questions.5.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. A painting cannot prove a conversation. It is easy to make one up. Look back at Lesson 13.
questions.5.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite. A painting cannot prove a conversation. It is easy to make up a conversation. Look at Lesson 13 again.

questions.5.options.2.feedback.source: Yes. We can describe what we see, such as where they look. Their thoughts stay unknown.
questions.5.options.2.feedback.back: Yes. We can describe what we see, such as where they are looking. Their thoughts remain unknown.

questions.6.question.source: Rodin shows six citizens side by side, all on one level. What does this choice show?
questions.6.question.back: Rodin shows six burghers side by side, all on one level. What does this choice show?
questions.6.question.note: "Citizens" is "warga kota", the word Lesson 14 uses for the burghers of Calais.

questions.6.options.0.text.back: The victory of one famous leader

questions.6.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. The town first planned a monument to one man. Rodin showed all six instead. Look back at Lesson 14.
questions.6.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite. The town first planned a monument to one man. Rodin showed all six. Look at Lesson 14 again.

questions.6.options.1.text.back: The power that England's king had

questions.6.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. The king is not in the sculpture. It shows six citizens facing a hard choice. Look back at Lesson 14.
questions.6.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite. The king is not in the sculpture. It shows six burghers facing a hard choice. Look at Lesson 14 again.

questions.6.options.2.feedback.source: Yes. Showing all six made the monument about a shared act. Each man reacts in his own way.
questions.6.options.2.feedback.back: Yes. By showing all six, the monument became about one shared act. Each man reacts in his own way.

questions.7.stimulus.body.source: This is a made-up example. Bronze statue of a sailor. It remembers a great storm in the year 1650. The artist made the model in 1900. This bronze cast was made from the model in 1990.
questions.7.stimulus.body.back: This is a made-up example. Bronze statue of a sailor. It commemorates a great storm in the year 1650. The artist made its model in 1900. This bronze cast was made from that model in 1990.

questions.7.question.source: When was this bronze statue itself made?
questions.7.question.back: When was this bronze statue itself made?

questions.7.options.0.feedback.source: Yes. The model came first. The bronze cast was made much later, in 1990.
questions.7.options.0.feedback.back: Yes. The model was made first. The bronze cast was made much later, in 1990.

questions.7.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. The storm is what the statue remembers. The bronze was made long after. Look back at Lesson 14.
questions.7.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite. The storm is what the statue commemorates. The bronze was made long after that. Look at Lesson 14 again.

questions.7.options.2.text.source: In 1900, when the model was made
questions.7.options.2.text.back: In 1900, when the model was made

questions.7.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. The model was made in 1900. The bronze cast came later. Look back at Lesson 14.
questions.7.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite. The model was made in 1900. The bronze cast came later. Look at Lesson 14 again.

questions.8.question.source: In Pieneman's painting, Dutch officers stand high under a raised flag. What does this choice do?
questions.8.question.back: In Pieneman's painting, Dutch officers stand high under a raised flag. What is the effect of this choice?

questions.8.options.0.text.source: It shows how Diponegoro felt inside.

questions.8.options.0.feedback.source: Not quite. A painted face or pose cannot prove what a person felt. Look back at Lesson 15.
questions.8.options.0.feedback.back: Not quite. A painted face or pose cannot prove a person's feelings. Look at Lesson 15 again.

questions.8.options.1.text.source: It makes Dutch power look certain.
questions.8.options.1.text.back: It makes Dutch power look certain.

questions.8.options.1.feedback.source: Yes. The painting was made for General De Kock. The tall officers and the flag make Dutch power look sure.
questions.8.options.1.feedback.back: Yes. The painting was made for General De Kock. The officers standing tall and the flag make Dutch power look certain.

questions.8.options.2.text.source: It questions the power of the Dutch.
questions.8.options.2.text.back: It questions the power of the Dutch.

questions.8.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. Saleh's later painting is the one scholars see as a challenge. Look back at Lesson 15.
questions.8.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite. Saleh's later painting is the painting that scholars see as a challenge. Look at Lesson 15 again.

questions.9.stimulus.title.source: Two made-up paintings of one boat race
questions.9.stimulus.title.back: Two made-up paintings of one boat race

questions.9.stimulus.body.source: This is a made-up example. A boat race took place in the made-up town of Pellam. The winning captain paid a painter to show the race. Years later, a second painter showed the same race from the losing crew's side.
questions.9.stimulus.body.back: This is a made-up example. A boat race was held in the made-up town of Pellam. The captain of the winning team paid a painter to paint the race. Years later, a second painter painted the same race from the losing team's side.

questions.9.question.source: Which question is most useful to ask about the first painting?
questions.9.question.back: Which question is most useful to ask about the first painting?

questions.9.options.0.text.source: Who paid for it, and why?
questions.9.options.0.text.back: Who paid for it, and why?

questions.9.options.0.feedback.source: Yes. A commission matters. The captain paid for it, so it may show the race his way.
questions.9.options.0.feedback.back: Yes. The commission matters. It was the captain who paid for it, so the painting may show the race from his point of view.

questions.9.options.1.text.source: Is it bigger than the other one?
questions.9.options.1.text.back: Is it bigger than the other one?

questions.9.options.1.feedback.source: Not quite. Size does not tell you whose view it shows. Ask who it was made for. Look back at Lesson 15.
questions.9.options.1.feedback.back: Not quite. Size does not tell you whose view it shows. Ask who it was made for. Look at Lesson 15 again.

questions.9.options.2.text.source: What colour is the captain's coat?
questions.9.options.2.text.back: What colour is the captain's coat?

questions.9.options.2.feedback.source: Not quite. That is a small detail. Ask who paid for it and why. Look back at Lesson 15.
questions.9.options.2.feedback.back: Not quite. That is a small detail. Ask who paid for it and why. Look at Lesson 15 again.
